paragraphs.heading: Two broad origins
paragraphs.text: An island is a piece of land, distinct from a continent, with water all around it. No standard of size separates islands from continents. Continents instead have an accepted geological definition: each is the largest landmass of a particular tectonic plate. By origin, there are continental islands and oceanic islands. Continental islands were split off a continent by plate tectonics, while oceanic islands have never belonged to one.

paragraphs.heading: Chains made over a hotspot
paragraphs.text: Islands often come in collections called archipelagos or island chains. Such chains are believed to arise from volcanic hotspots, places in the lithosphere where the mantle is hotter than the area around it. A hotspot gives rise to volcanoes, and their lava becomes the rock the islands are made of. For some islands, tectonic plates moving above a stationary hotspot would form a linear chain. Islands further from the hotspot are progressively older and more eroded, and in the end they vanish beneath the sea entirely. The Hawaiian Islands are an example: the oldest island is 25 million years old, and the youngest, Hawaii, is still an active volcano.

paragraphs.heading: Chains made all at once
paragraphs.text: Not every island chain forms this way. Some may be created in one go, when fractures in the tectonic plates themselves produce multiple islands simultaneously. The Line Islands are one supporting piece of evidence. Rather than having different ages, all of them are estimated to be 8 million years old.

paragraphs.heading: Pieces of continents
paragraphs.text: Other island chains form by being separated from existing continents. The Japanese archipelago may have been separated from Eurasia by seafloor spreading, in which new oceanic crust forms and pushes older crust away. Islands that sit on the continental shelf may be called continental islands. Some islands, such as the ones that make up New Zealand, are what is left of continents that shrank and sank under the sea. New Zealand sits on Zealandia, a continent-like area of crust, and an estimated 93% of Zealandia's original surface area has been submerged.

paragraphs.heading: Coral, sediment and human hands
paragraphs.text: Coral builds islands too. Some form when reefs grow on volcanic islands that have sunk below the surface. Where such coral islands ring a central lagoon, the island is called an atoll. Sediment building up in shallow patches of water helps reefs, and the islands related to them, to form. Sediment along shorelines can also create barrier islands, and sediment and debris in rivers can form river islands. Artificial islands are those made by humans, and they include large-scale land reclamation projects used for development.

paragraphs.heading: What origin means for island life
paragraphs.text: Islands are home to diverse plant and animal life. Around an oceanic island the sea acts as a natural barrier that keeps new species from being introduced, and this causes the species that do arrive to evolve in isolation. A continental island shares animal and plant life with the continent it split from. Depending on how long ago that island formed, its life may have diverged greatly from the mainland through natural selection.
